description: We are a multidisciplinary team interested in science, engineering, technology, and space exploration. Our interests include physics, programming, robotics, and problem-solving, and we are motivated by the opportunity to apply scientific knowledge to challenges of the real world.
summary:
Project Phoenix is an educational browser game for children aged 7–14, developed in response to NASA’s challenge to make the decisions behind real space missions more engaging and accessible. Players take command of a Martian outpost and have four nights to prepare it for the arrival of its first human colonists.

Throughout the game with a 2.5D gameplay style, made to be similar to the game FNAF 6, proven to be engaging and intuitive for young audiences (that game has a 93% approval rating), players manage essential resources such as water, oxygen, food, and energy, maintain life-support systems, solve emergencies, and upgrade the base. Gameplay combines nighttime shifts focused on resource management with daytime shifts dedicated to improvements. Guided by YANA, a friendly robotic companion, players also complete interactive quizzes that teach scientific concepts and reward correct answers with energy points.

Project Phoenix integrates real NASA resources, including solar-flare data from DONKI, which influences its final challenge. It also features a custom 3D map of the Martian base and cinematic dream sequences of the main character that gradually reveal the mystery behind Earth's collapse and the role of aerosols.

By combining real scientific data, strategic gameplay, and interactive storytelling, Project Phoenix encourages young players to explore space science, develop problem-solving skills, and understand the challenges of human colonization beyond Earth.
details:
Project Phoenix: Project Details

Project Phoenix is a free browser game for children aged 7 to 14. Players take on the role of the commander of humanity's first Mars base in 2071, where they must keep essential systems running for four nights, managing water, oxygen, food, and energy. Along the way, they discover the real science behind the machines that keep the base alive, while a real solar flare recorded in NASA's DONKI database drives the final night's challenge.

What it does and how it works

Story

In 2071, the player wakes up as the commander of the Central Superbase, humanity's first permanent settlement on Mars and the heart of Project Phoenix: a plan to survive after Earth's sky was overwhelmed by smoke, aerosols, and acid rain.

YANA, the base's AI companion, introduces the player to their role, explains why they are there, and shows what the base needs to survive. Through three short dream videos featuring memories of Earth, players gradually discover how the planet's own life-support systems broke down, and why they now have to produce every breath of air and every drop of water themselves.

How the game works

The game takes place over four nights, each following the same cycle:

1. Night – Managing the base

Players move between five rooms: Water, Oxygen, Food (greenhouse), Energy, and Control. Each essential resource has its own bar, showing its current level, target, production rate, and storage capacity.

Machines can break down, and players must repair them through short minigames. These problems include a clogged water filter, a frozen pipe, a failed electrolyzer, a full CO₂ filter, wilted plants, and dusty solar panels.

When everything is running smoothly, players can choose to wait one hour, allowing time to pass. Resource costs are calculated at the end of each hour.

2. Report and bedtime question

At the end of the night, players receive a report showing what was produced and what was lost. YANA then asks a short science question about something that happened during the game.

3. Dream

A short story video plays, revealing another memory of Earth. When it ends, the commander wakes up and the base gradually comes back into view.

4. Day – Planning and improvements

During the day, players get an overhead view of the base and can spend their resources on 26 upgrades inspired by real or planned space technologies.

These include:

• Water: storage tanks, an ice drill, and a water recycler.

• Oxygen: additional electrolyzers and MOXIE.

• Food: hydroponic shelves, LED grow lights, and a cold pantry.

• Energy: batteries, solar panels, a mini reactor, and a cleaning robot.

• Protection: pre-filters and radiation shielding for equipment.

Increasing challenges

Each night introduces something new:

• Night 1: A guided tutorial where YANA points out the least-filled resource bar and explains the controls.

• Night 2: Random equipment failures begin to appear.

• Night 3: A Martian sandstorm reduces solar panel output by half and spreads dust throughout the rooms.

• Night 4: The final challenge begins with a real solar flare from NASA's DONKI database, displayed on the Control screen. It triggers a solar storm that causes communication loss, equipment failures, and red emergency lighting. Players who previously purchased Equipment Shielding can reduce the damage, just as shielding helps protect real equipment.

The ending depends on how well players have managed and maintained the base throughout all four nights. After the Night 4 report, a short cinematic shows the first colonists arriving on Mars. Then the screen goes black and a story crawl rises slowly: "Once upon a time, humanity had a perfect home...". It retells how humanity wasted Earth's air, water and soil, and then, depending on the ending, what happened to the mission and to humanity's future. It fades into a large GOOD ENDING, MID ENDING or BAD ENDING card, followed by a summary of the player's upgrades, answers and facts learned.

How it runs

• Free and accessible: Project Phoenix is a static web page that runs in any modern browser, with no installation or account required. It is hosted on GitHub Pages: https://alexgam347.github.io/ProjectPhoenix/

• Saved progress: Game progress is stored in the browser, allowing players to continue their game later.

• Language: The game is in English, with subtitles available for the dream videos.

• Accessibility options: Players can adjust sound settings and reduce flashing effects.

Benefits and intended impact

Benefits for players (ages 7–14)

Learning by doing, rather than just reading. Instead of simply memorizing that an electrolyzer separates water into oxygen, children can see the oxygen level drop when the machine loses power and then repair it themselves. Each scientific concept is connected to something that happens in the game.

Understanding how systems work together. Water, oxygen, food, and energy all depend on one another:

• Melting ice requires energy.

• Producing oxygen requires water.

• Plants need water, light, and CO₂.

• Storage capacity is limited.

Players gradually discover that keeping a base alive means balancing several interconnected systems, not just maintaining individual machines.

Real science in small, understandable steps. Each night introduces only a few new ideas through YANA's explanations, upgrade descriptions, and a short bedtime question. These questions reinforce what players have learned without making the experience feel like a test.

Real NASA data. The final night is based on the strongest real solar flare recorded in the previous 12 months, downloaded from NASA's DONKI database each time the game is built. Players can see its actual date and discover that space weather is monitored and recorded every day.

Free and easy to access. The game can be played on school or home computers through a browser, with no installation, account, advertisements, or in-app purchases.

Intended impact

1. Connecting Mars to Earth.

One of the game's central messages is that nothing on Mars comes for free: every breath of air and every drop of water must be produced and carefully managed. On Earth, our atmosphere, water cycle, and soil provide many of these essentials naturally, but human activities can damage these systems. Through the dream sequences, players discover how Earth's life-support systems can break down, with real NASA satellite missions such as Terra and Aqua (MODIS), SMAP, FIRMS, and Aura helping illustrate these changes.

2. Inspiring interest in STEM and space exploration.

Engineering, botany, planetary science, and space weather all become part of the challenges players must solve, helping them discover how different scientific fields contribute to space exploration.

3. Supporting teachers and classroom learning.

Each night's gameplay takes only a few minutes, making it easier to fit into a classroom session. Teachers can also use YANA's bedtime questions and the credits page, which explains the sources behind the game's scientific information, as starting points for classroom discussions.

4. Encouraging care for Earth's climate and atmosphere.

Ultimately, we want players to leave with a simple but important idea: protecting Earth's natural life-support systems is much easier than having to rebuild them on another planet.

How NASA data is used

NASA data is used in three ways: live data inside the game, sources that shaped the rules and rooms, and the satellite missions cited in the dream videos.

1. Live data in the game: NASA DONKI

• What: the strongest solar flare (class, peak time and active region) recorded in the last 12 months, from the DONKI Space Weather Database (NASA Community Coordinated Modeling Center), queried through NASA Open APIs (api.nasa.gov).

• How: a build script (scripts/fetch-donki.mjs) downloads it each time the game is built and deployed. If the API is unreachable, the game uses a real backup flare: class X9.0, peak 3 October 2024 12:18 UTC, active region 13842.

• Where: Night 4 opens on the Control screen with that flare. The story year is 2071 (same day and month), and the real date is shown below as "real data: NASA DONKI". The flare starts the solar storm: four rooms fail, or only two with the Equipment Shielding upgrade, and solar efficiency drops to 63% (86% with shielding).

How to explain each idea simply

3. NASA missions cited in the dream videos

The three dreams are fiction set in Earth's future, built on real NASA Earth-observing missions and real events:

• Terra and Aqua (MODIS) measure aerosol optical depth, the amount of smoke and particles in the air.

• SMAP measures soil moisture from space.

• FIRMS maps active fires worldwide.

• Aura measures sulfur dioxide and nitrogen dioxide, the gases behind acid rain.

• NASA Earth Observatory published the Blue Marble image and the reports on Pinatubo, pyrocumulonimbus clouds and acid rain.

Every citation, with its timestamp, is listed under References and sources.

How the project is creative

• A survival-management game for kids. Project Phoenix takes inspiration from survival-management games, using a simple cycle: survive the night, then plan and improve the base during the day. However, instead of jump scares or frightening enemies, the challenges come from keeping the base running. Frozen pipes, Martian dust, sandstorms, and solar flares create tension while keeping the experience suitable for younger players.

• Real data changes the game. The final night's solar storm is not simply a scripted event. It is based on the strongest real solar flare recorded in the previous 12 months. This means the game can change as solar activity changes, allowing players to encounter a real event and its actual date from NASA's records within a fictional story set in 2071.

• Mars as a mirror of Earth. The story introduces an unexpected idea: humanity did not leave Earth simply to explore another planet, but because it damaged its own life-support systems. Through the dream sequences, players gradually discover what happened. These videos draw on real NASA Earth-observation missions, connecting the challenges of surviving on Mars with the importance of protecting our own planet.

• Science as mechanics, not quizzes. Each upgrade is real or planned technology (MOXIE, Veggie-style LED lights, fission surface power, ISS-style water recycling). Similarly, the equipment failures reflect challenges associated with operating systems in the Martian environment. Players learn because understanding these systems helps them keep the base alive.

• A character who teaches. YANA, the base's AI companion, guides players through the mission using short, retro-style dialogue boxes. She introduces the story after the opening sequence, guides players through their first night, and shares scientific facts one at a time. This keeps explanations short and makes learning feel like part of the adventure rather than a separate lesson.

• A consistent retro art direction:

◦ 3D renders of the base made in Blender;

◦ a pixel-art Mars menu made from the team's own image;

◦ a CRT terminal style;

◦ cinematic dream videos with subtitles;

◦ public-domain space music ("Pondering the Cosmos" by Ruskerdax).

Factors the team considered

• Age range (7 to 14):

◦ short sentences and one idea per fact;

◦ a guided first night;

◦ no reading walls;

◦ no gore or horror;

◦ tension without fear.

A text rule, checked by an automated test, keeps the player-facing text simple and free of long dashes and separator symbols.

• Scientific accuracy versus story:

◦ The game mechanics and YANA's facts follow NASA sources (see References and sources).

◦ The dreams and the epilogue are clearly fiction about a possible future, built on real NASA missions.

◦ Some story elements are dramatized for impact, such as Dream 1's aerosol optical depth of 5.0 "over all continents". For comparison, the 1991 Pinatubo eruption reached about 0.15 and Tambora in 1815 about 0.45.

• Balance and fairness: a bot plays the game across many random seeds in the automated tests, so every night can be won by a careful player and the endings depend on choices, not luck. Costs are charged at the end of each hour, and storage is limited, so producing more than you can store is wasted, as in real life support.

• Accessibility and reach:

◦ runs in the browser on low-end school computers;

◦ subtitles on all three dream videos;

◦ an option to reduce flashing effects, which also flattens the epilogue crawl;

◦ sound starts only after the player chooses it;

◦ keyboard controls for dialog, and SKIP on every video and on the epilogue;

◦ an MP3 fallback for older Safari.

• Data reliability: We wanted the final challenge to work even if NASA's API becomes temporarily unavailable. For this reason, if the API cannot be accessed when the game is built, a backup based on a real solar flare is used instead. This ensures that the game remains playable without losing its scientific foundation.

• Honesty and rules:

◦ The Use of AI is declared in the game, the README, the repository and this submission, and the dream videos and the finale cinematic are labeled "AI assisted".

◦ No NASA logos or insignia are used, and AI content is not presented as NASA material.

◦ The required NASA non-endorsement notice appears in the credits.

• Licences and original work:

◦ all music, fonts, software and voices are public domain or open source;

◦ all 3D renders and the menu image are the team's own work.

Use of AI

Project Phoenix was designed and directed by our team. We developed the concept, story, characters, game design and balancing, 3D base and room renders using Blender, the scripts and direction of the dream videos and the finale cinematic, and the selection of NASA data.

The game's programming code was entirely AI-generated. Claude (Anthropic) produced the code based on our design document and detailed, step-by-step instructions. Claude also helped draft the in-game English text and generate the dream videos and the finale cinematic following our scripts and visual direction. The voices in the dream videos were generated using Kokoro-82M, an open-source text-to-speech model.

Throughout development, we tested each change and requested corrections until the results matched our intended design. The dream videos and the finale cinematic are clearly labeled "AI assisted" within the game.

We do not use NASA logos or branding, and no AI-generated content is presented as official NASA material.

E. Notes from the video check

• "NASA Science Note" boxes (Dreams 2 and 3). They are text boxes that cite NASA missions, not NASA logos or insignia. Because they appear inside AI-assisted video, mention in the submission that they are the team's own captions, not official NASA material. Another option is to rename them "Science Note" in a future edit.

• New Dream 1. The 15-second version keeps the Terra and Aqua (MODIS) reference, now in the narration, the subtitles and the on-screen ticker. Tambora, Pinatubo and acid rain are no longer mentioned in Dream 1; acid rain is still covered in Dream 3 and in the epilogue.

• Dramatization. Dream 1's "aerosol optical depth at 5.0 over all continents" is fiction for impact; real large eruptions reached about 0.15 (Pinatubo) to 0.45 (Tambora).

• Veggie lights. Veggie uses red and blue LEDs, plus green so crews can see the plants. The game's "mostly red and blue" is correct.

• Story dates. Dream 2 is a memory set before the departure. The game takes place in 2071, and the Night 4 flare shows 2071 with the real NASA date below it.

• Finale and epilogue. The finale cinematic has no narration or data. The epilogue text is the team's story, not a source claim.

Ready-to-paste version (Project Details field)

Project Phoenix is a free browser game for ages 7 to 14. In 2071 the player wakes up as commander of the first permanent Mars base, the heart of Project Phoenix, humanity's backup after Earth's sky was choked by smoke, aerosols and acid rain. Over four nights the player keeps water, oxygen, food and energy running across five rooms. They fix faults like frozen pipes, clogged filters and dusty solar panels, and survive a Martian sandstorm and a solar storm. Between nights they answer a science question, watch a dream about how Earth's life support broke down, and buy upgrades based on real technology: MOXIE, ISS-style water recycling, Veggie-style LED grow lights, batteries and a fission reactor. YANA, the base's AI companion, guides the first night and shares short facts. At the end, the colonists land and a story epilogue tells whether humanity was saved, before the good, mid or bad ending.

NASA data: every build downloads the strongest real solar flare of the past 12 months from NASA DONKI through NASA Open APIs. That flare opens Night 4 on the Control screen, with its real date, and triggers the solar storm. RadLab radiation data shaped the shielding upgrade. ECLSS, OSDR lettuce studies, Veggie and the CSA food kit shaped the water, oxygen and greenhouse rooms. Mars Trek guided the base site. The dreams cite NASA Terra and Aqua (MODIS), SMAP, FIRMS, Aura and Earth Observatory.

Benefits and impact: children learn by doing that life support is a balance of connected systems, and that Earth gives us for free what we would have to build on Mars. The game is free, needs no install and fits in a class session.

Tools: TypeScript, HTML and CSS, Vite, Vitest (76 automated tests including a balance bot), Node.js scripts, sharp, ffmpeg, Playwright, GitHub Actions and Pages, Blender (team renders), Kokoro-82M (voices) and public-domain music by Ruskerdax.

Use of AI: the team designed and directed everything: concept, story, characters, game design and balance, Blender renders, video scripts and choice of NASA data. The programming code was entirely AI generated by Claude (Anthropic) from our design and step-by-step instructions.
